a: Do not give him free rein in his youth

t: A longer verse in the Hebrew and Latin
p: The Hebrew and Latin begin with 'Bow his head (neck) in his youth'. The variant at the end of the verse goes with this one.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew's extra line is a common Hebrew pairing (head and loins); the Greek translator, or the copyists after him, kept only one line.

a: or he may grow hard and refuse to obey you
t: A closing line: 'grief to you from him'
p: The Hebrew and Latin end the verse with grief for the father. It goes with the variant at the start of the verse.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete

readings.plain: or he may grow hard and refuse to obey you

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 30:12; similarly the Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 30:12 and the KJV

readings.plain: or he may grow hard and refuse to obey you, / and you will have grief from him

why: The Plain follows the Greek, its base text.

a: so that he does not stumble and disgrace you
p: Vaticanus speaks of 'your' disgrace; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi of 'his' shameful conduct, which trips you up.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἵνα μὴ ἐν τῇ ἀσχημοσύνῃ σου προσκόψῃ
readings.en: so that he does not stumble, to your shame
readings.plain: so that he does not stumble and disgrace you

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A) and Ephraemi (C), as Swete's notes give them; the KJV ("lest his lewd behaviour be an offence unto thee") and the Latin agree in sense
readings.orig: ἵνα μὴ ἐν τῇ ἀσχημοσύνῃ αὐτοῦ προσκόψῃς
readings.en: so that you do not stumble over his shameful conduct
readings.plain: so that his shameful ways do not trip you up

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus, its base text; the meaning is close either way. The other codices read more smoothly, which may be why they changed the pronouns.
b: Codex Ephraemi also has "while he is a child" in place of "and work hard at him," a line taken from the verse before.

a: or than a sickness that never leaves
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus, the Hebrew and the Latin read 'and eternal rest' is better than lasting sickness.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete; first hand of Sinaiticus; Alexandrinus; Ephraemi; the KJV
readings.orig: κρείσσων θάνατος ὑπὲρ ζωὴν πικρὰν ἢ ἀρρώστημα ἔμμονον
readings.en: Death is better than a bitter life or a lasting illness
readings.plain: or than a sickness that never leaves

readings.w: A corrector of Sinaiticus (ℵc.a), adding καὶ ἀνάπαυσις αἰώνιος; Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 30:17; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 30:17 (requies aeterna)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀνάπαυσις αἰώνιος ... ἢ ἀρρώστημα ἔμμονον
readings.en: and eternal rest (is better) than a lasting illness
readings.plain: and eternal rest than a sickness that never leaves

why: The Plain follows its base text. The Hebrew shows that 'eternal rest' was in Ben Sira's original; the corrector of Sinaiticus brought the Greek closer to it. 'Eternal rest' here means the sleep of death, not a heavenly reward.

a: So it is with the one whom the Lord is hounding.
t: The sick man, or the rich man?
p: The Greek compares the sick man to an idol at a feast; the Hebrew compares a rich man who cannot enjoy his wealth.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices
readings.en: So is the one pursued by the Lord
readings.plain: So it is with the one whom the Lord is hounding.

readings.en: So is one who has wealth and does not enjoy it
readings.plain: So it is with one who has wealth / and gets no pleasure from it.

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 30:20; Douay-Rheims
readings.orig: Sic qui effugatur a Domino, portans mercedes iniquitatis
readings.en: So is he that is driven away by the Lord, bearing the reward of iniquity
readings.plain: So it is with the one whom the Lord drives away, / carrying the wages of his wrongdoing.

why: The Plain follows the Greek, which Catholic and Orthodox churches received. The Hebrew line fits the setting of food (30:18) and may be Ben Sira's own; the Greek turns it toward sickness as God's punishment.

a: like a eunuch who holds a young woman in his arms and groans
t: An added line: 'so is one who does justice by force'
p: A later hand in Vaticanus and the Hebrew add the line found at 20:4.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete (the first hand), with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus

readings.plain: like a eunuch who holds a young woman in his arms and groans

readings.en: so is the one who does justice by force
readings.plain: like a eunuch who holds a young woman in his arms and groans. / So is the one who does justice by force

why: The Plain follows the first hand. The added line is the end of 20:4 and probably came in from there, though the Hebrew has it here too.

a: treat him like yourself
p: Vaticanus repeats 'like yourself'; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, the Latin and the KJV say 'like a brother'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.en: treat him as yourself
readings.plain: treat him like yourself

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi, as Swete's notes give them; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 33:31 (quasi fratrem); the KJV (33:31, "entreat him as a brother")
readings.en: treat him as a brother
readings.plain: treat him like a brother

why: The Plain follows its base text. 'Brother' may be original, since Vaticanus's 'yourself' repeats the first line; but both readings say the same thing.

a: A well-taught man knows many things
p: Vaticanus reads 'a well-taught man'; Sinaiticus and the first hand of Alexandrinus read 'a man who has traveled'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete; a corrector of Alexandrinus
readings.en: An educated man knew many things
readings.plain: A well-taught man knows many things

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and, it seems, the first hand of Alexandrinus (Swete's notes); the KJV (34:9, "A man that hath travelled")
readings.en: A man who has wandered knew many things
readings.plain: A man who has traveled knows many things

why: The Plain follows its base text. 'Traveled' fits 31:10–12, where the same verb ("wandered") follows, and may be original; 'taught' fits the book's praise of learning. The two words differ by a few letters in Greek.

a: an offering made in mockery
p: Alexandrinus reads 'blemished' for 'mocked', and so does the Latin. The variant in 31:22 goes with this one.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with Sinaiticus

readings.plain: an offering made in mockery

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes); Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 34:21 (maculata)
readings.en: a blemished offering
readings.plain: an offering with a blemish

why: The Plain follows its base text. 'Blemished' fits the language of sacrifice (offerings had to be without blemish, Leviticus 22:20); the two Greek words differ by one letter.

a: the mockeries of lawless men
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read 'blemishes'; a note in Sinaiticus's margin reads 'gifts'. Goes with 31:21.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.en: mockeries of the lawless
readings.plain: the mockeries of lawless men

readings.plain: the blemished gifts of lawless men

readings.w: A marginal note in Sinaiticus (Swete's notes); the KJV (34:18, "the gifts of unjust men")
readings.en: gifts of the lawless
readings.plain: the gifts of lawless men

why: The Plain follows its base text, keeping the wordplay with 31:21.

a: Have mercy on us, Master, God of all
p: Alexandrinus leaves out 'Master'; the Hebrew begins 'Save us, God of all'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with Sinaiticus

readings.plain: Have mercy on us, Master, God of all

readings.plain: Have mercy on us, God of all

readings.plain: Save us, God of all

why: The Plain follows its base text. The Hebrew 'save us' is the cry of Psalm 106:47; the Greek 'have mercy' is the opening of many prayers.

a: cast the fear of you on all the nations
t: 'The nations that have not sought you'
p: The Latin and the KJV add 'that have not sought you'. The Greek and the Hebrew do not.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 35:1 ("lift up your terror over all the nations")
readings.orig: ἐπίβαλε τὸν φόβον σου ἐπὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη
readings.en: cast your fear on all the nations
readings.plain: cast the fear of you on all the nations

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:2; the KJV (36:2, "that seek not after thee")
readings.orig: immitte timorem tuum super gentes quæ non exquisierunt te
readings.en: send your fear on the nations that have not sought you
readings.plain: cast the fear of you on all the nations that have not sought you

why: The Plain follows the Greek; the Hebrew agrees with it in having no limit. The Latin narrows the prayer to the nations that do not seek God.

a: Hurry the time and remember your oath
p: The Hebrew asks God to hurry 'the end' and appoint 'the set time'; the Latin says 'remember the end'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices
readings.en: Hasten the time and remember the oath
readings.plain: Hurry the time and remember your oath

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 35:7

readings.en: Hasten the end and appoint the set time, for who can say to you, 'What are you doing?'
readings.plain: Hurry the end and appoint the set time

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:10; the KJV (36:8, "remember the covenant")
readings.en: Hasten the time, and remember the end
readings.plain: Hurry the time and remember the end

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew's 'end' (qets) and 'set time' (mo'ed) are the words of Habakkuk 2:3 and Daniel 8:19; the Hebrew also adds a line that the Greek lacks.

a: Smash the heads of the enemy's rulers
p: Where the Greek has 'rulers of the enemies', the Hebrew names Moab, in the words of Balaam's oracle.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:12; the KJV (36:10, "the rulers of the heathen")
readings.en: Crush the heads of the rulers of enemies
readings.plain: Smash the heads of the enemy's rulers

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 35:8
readings.en: Put an end to the head of the brows of Moab
readings.plain: Make an end of the brows of Moab

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew takes up Numbers 24:17, "It will smash the brows of Moab," with 'Moab' as a name for Israel's enemies; its second line is singular, "who says, 'There is no one but me.'" The grandson, writing for readers in Egypt, made the prayer general.
b: Moab had long ceased to be a power in Ben Sira's time, so the Hebrew uses it as a code name, as Isaiah 25:10 and Balaam's oracle do. Some scholars think it stands for the Seleucid empire.

a: trips up those who sacrifice to it
t: 'Sacrifice to it' or 'are mad about it'?
p: Vaticanus reads 'sacrifice to it'; the first hand of Sinaiticus reads 'are possessed by it'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete; a corrector of Sinaiticus; the KJV (31:7, "them that sacrifice unto it")
readings.en: to those who sacrifice to it
readings.plain: trips up those who sacrifice to it

readings.w: The first hand of Sinaiticus (Swete's notes)
readings.en: to those who are wildly devoted to it
readings.plain: trips up those who are mad about it

why: The Plain follows its base text. The two Greek words differ by one letter; 'mad about it' (the root of English 'enthusiasm') may be the grandson's word, but 'sacrifice' fits the picture of gold as an idol.

a: will accept discipline
p: Swete prints Vaticanus's spelling paidian, 'play'; the corrected Vaticanus and Alexandrinus spell paideian, 'discipline'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, first hand, as printed by Swete
readings.en: will receive play
readings.plain: will accept play

readings.w: Correctors of Vaticanus (Bᵃᵇ) and Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes); the KJV (32:14, "his discipline"); Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 32:14 (מוסר)
readings.en: will receive discipline
readings.plain: will accept discipline

why: In the codices of this period the letters ει and ι were pronounced alike and often confused, so the first hand's paidian is a spelling of paideian. The Hebrew musar, 'discipline', confirms the sense.

a: and watch out for your own children
p: The Greek says 'guard yourself from your children'; the Hebrew says 'be careful in your paths'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 32:26; the KJV (32:22)

readings.en: and guard yourself from your children
readings.plain: and watch out for your own children

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 32:22 (the line is also given at his 32:21 as "guard your end")
readings.en: and be careful in your paths
readings.plain: and be careful on your paths

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew fits the road picture of 35:20–21 better and is probably Ben Sira's own; see the note on the word.

a: In everything you do, trust yourself
p: The Greek says 'trust your soul'; the Hebrew says 'guard your soul'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; the KJV (32:23, "trust thy own soul")
readings.orig: ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ πίστευε τῇ ψυχῇ σου
readings.en: in every work trust your soul
readings.plain: In everything you do, trust yourself

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 32:22–23
readings.en: in all your deeds guard yourself
readings.plain: In everything you do, guard yourself

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew 'guard' fits the warnings of 35:20–22; in Greek the verbs for 'guard' and 'trust' are not alike, so the grandson probably read a different Hebrew word, or chose to say it differently.

a: as an inquiry made by the righteous
p: Vaticanus reads 'of the righteous'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read the Septuagint word for the Urim; the Hebrew names the Urim.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete
readings.en: as an inquiry of the righteous
readings.plain: as an inquiry made by the righteous

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes)
readings.en: as an inquiry of the Urim
readings.plain: as an inquiry made by the Urim

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 33:3
readings.en: and his law is like the Urim in the breastpiece
readings.plain: as the Urim in the breastpiece

why: The Plain follows its base text. Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus are very likely right: their δήλων is the Septuagint's word for the Urim (Numbers 27:21), and the Hebrew says so plainly. Δικαίων, 'of the righteous', looks like a copyist's change to a commoner word.

a: and you will give them their inheritance as at the beginning
t: 'You will give them' or 'I gave them'?
p: Swete prints a corrected text here; Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read 'I gave them their inheritance'.

readings.w: Swete's text (a correction he explains in his preface); Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:13 (et hæreditabis eos); the KJV (36:11, "and inherit thou them")

readings.plain: and you will give them their inheritance as at the beginning

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 35:9

readings.plain: and let them take their inheritance as in days of old

why: The three great codices have 'I', which came in because this half-line now follows 'I too kept watch' (see the note). Swete's correction to 'you' restores the prayer's sense, which the Hebrew and the Latin confirm.

a: with the praise of your mighty deeds
t: 'Praise of your deeds', 'lift up your oracles' or 'your majesty'?
p: Vaticanus reads one rare word; correctors and other codices split it into 'to lift up your oracles'; the Hebrew says 'your majesty'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete (first hand)
readings.en: fill Zion with the telling of your mighty deeds
readings.plain: with the praise of your mighty deeds

readings.w: A corrector of Vaticanus, Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes)

readings.en: fill Zion, to lift up your oracles
readings.plain: so it may lift up your oracles

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:16; the KJV (36:14, "thine unspeakable oracles")
readings.en: Fill Zion with your words beyond telling
readings.plain: with your words beyond telling

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 35:12
readings.en: Fill Zion with your majesty
readings.plain: with your majesty

why: The Plain follows its base text. Aretalogia, the recital of a god's mighty deeds, was a rare word; later copyists divided its letters into commoner words, which gave the KJV's 'oracles'.

a: fill your people with your glory
p: The Greek has 'your people'; the Hebrew has 'your temple'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:16; the KJV

readings.en: and your people from your glory
readings.plain: fill your people with your glory

readings.plain: fill your temple with your glory

why: The Plain follows the Greek. In Greek 'people' (laon) and 'temple' (naon) differ by one letter, so a copyist's slip early in the Greek is likely; the Hebrew, with Zion in the first line, points to the temple, as in Haggai 2:7.

a: the prayer of those who plead with you
p: Vaticanus reads 'suppliants'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read 'servants', as do the Latin, the Hebrew and the KJV.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete

readings.plain: the prayer of those who plead with you

readings.en: the prayer of your servants
readings.plain: the prayer of your servants

why: The Plain follows its base text. The two Greek words differ by one letter, and the Hebrew 'your servants' supports the reading of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus.

a: as Aaron blessed your people.
p: The Greek and the Latin speak of the blessing of Aaron; the Hebrew says 'according to your goodwill toward your people'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed by Swete, with the other codices; Latin Vulgate (Clementine) 36:19; the KJV (36:17)
readings.orig: κατὰ τὴν εὐλογίαν Ἀαρὼν περὶ τοῦ λαοῦ σου

readings.plain: as Aaron blessed your people.

readings.w: Hebrew of the Cairo Genizah copies, in Kahana's edition (1912), his 35:15
readings.en: according to your goodwill toward your people
readings.plain: in your goodwill toward your people.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew is simpler; the Greek may come from a Hebrew copy that read birkat, 'blessing', or from the grandson's wish to name the priestly blessing.
